books.section: Topic 8.13 The environment and natural resources from 1968 to 1980
The Dangers of Nuclear Energy and Three Mile Island

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note); the table is from the U.S. Energy Information Administration; the photographs are public domain

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the environmental movement changed American politics from 1962 to 1980.

documents.title: A silent spring
documents.source: Paraphrase of Rachel Carson, Silent Spring (Houghton Mifflin, 1962).
documents.sourcing: Carson wrote as a scientist warning the public, so her book argues from evidence about wildlife rather than from politics.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, published September 27, 1962. Carson, a marine biologist, warned that the pesticide DDT and other chemicals were poisoning the natural world. She described how DDT built up in the bodies of animals, thinned the shells of birds' eggs, and spread through food chains from insects to fish to birds.

documents.title: Oil on the water
documents.source: Photograph: aerial view of oil rising near Union Oil Platform A, Santa Barbara Channel, 1969, public domain (U.S. Geological Survey).
documents.sourcing: The aerial photograph shows the spill from above, so it records the scale of the disaster rather than its effects on shore.

documents.title: The first Earth Day
documents.source: Photograph: protesters at the Earth Day flag ceremony, Washington Monument, Washington, D.C., April 22, 1970, public domain (U.S. National Park Service).
documents.sourcing: The photograph was taken at a public ceremony, so it shows the movement presenting itself to the nation rather than working behind closed doors.

documents.title: A new agency
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Richard Nixon's message to Congress proposing the Environmental Protection Agency, July 9, 1970.
documents.sourcing: Nixon wrote as a president answering public pressure, so his proposal claims the issue for his administration.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Richard Nixon's message to Congress, July 9, 1970. Nixon proposed bringing the government's scattered environmental programs together into a single new agency, the Environmental Protection Agency, so that the fight against pollution would have one home in the federal government.

documents.title: The price of gasoline
documents.source: Table: average retail price of regular gasoline, U.S. Energy Information Administration.
documents.sourcing: The table gives yearly averages, so it shows the trend across the decade rather than the price on any single day.
documents.text: Average price of regular gasoline, cents per gallon (U.S. Energy Information Administration): 1973, 39 cents; 1974, 53 cents; 1979, 86 cents; 1980, 119 cents.

documents.title: A crisis of confidence
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Jimmy Carter's televised address on energy, July 15, 1979.
documents.sourcing: Carter spoke to the nation on television after days of seclusion at Camp David, so his address is a presidential appeal to the public, not a policy paper.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Jimmy Carter's televised address, July 15, 1979. Carter told Americans the country faced a 'crisis of confidence' that went deeper than the energy shortage. He set a goal of 20 percent of the nation's energy from solar power by the year 2000 and called every act of conservation an act of patriotism.

documents.title: The Sagebrush claim
documents.source: Paraphrase of Nevada Assembly Bill 413, enacted June 2, 1979.
documents.sourcing: The law is a state claim against the federal government, so it states Nevada's position in the strongest possible terms.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Nevada Assembly Bill 413, June 2, 1979. The Nevada legislature claimed title to the 48 million acres of federal land inside the state, about 79 percent of Nevada, arguing that the land had been meant to pass to the state.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the environmental movement changed American politics from 1962 to 1980, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the postwar growth of federal power, the rights movements of the 1960s, or the energy crises of the 1970s.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (first point): earns the point for describing specific examples from at least three documents that support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without using their content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (outside evidence): earns the point for describing at least one specific piece of evidence beyond the documents that supports the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Repeating a document's content as outside evidence does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience of at least one document shapes what it says.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how that shapes the document does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for showing a complex understanding, such as explaining both the change and its limits, or qualifying the argument with evidence that cuts the other way.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument with no qualification or counter-evidence does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The environmental movement changed American politics deeply from 1962 to 1980, but the change stayed partial.
Grouping: Documents 1-3 show the movement's rise (Carson, the Santa Barbara spill, Earth Day); Documents 4-6 show politics answering it (the EPA, gasoline prices, Carter's address); Document 7 shows the backlash (the Sagebrush claim).
Background: The Clean Air Act of 1970 set national air standards, the Clean Water Act of 1972 set federal limits on water pollution, and the Endangered Species Act of 1973 protected species and habitats.
Background: The Love Canal emergency of August 1978 then pushed Congress toward the Superfund law of December 1980.
Background: The same decade that created the EPA also produced the Sagebrush Rebellion and a president who called saving energy a patriotic duty yet lost re-election, so the movement remade the government's job while leaving its politics divided.
